newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Composer heads south for Antarctic symphony.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Composer heads south for Antarctic symphony.

text.p: Hours before conducting a new work at London's Royal Albert Hall, Sir Peter Maxwell Davies is trying on snow boots and ski suits ahead of a journey into the artistic unknown.
In an unusual experiment, the 62-year-old composer plans to spend a month in the Antarctic gaining inspiration for a sequel to the Sinfonia Antarctica written by Ralph Vaughan Williams in 1953.
Anyone who lives in a remote settlement on Hoy island off the northern tip of Scotland is used to barren wastes and has a healthy respect for the forces of nature.
But "Max" admits he is very daunted ahead of this trip of a lifetime.
"I'm game for anything, but of course I'm nervous about it. I hope I don't make a fool of myself with all the gear," Maxwell Davies said in an interview.
"I was a coastguard on Hoy for 10 years but I was never very good. I'm sure people will be very kind and they'll realise composers are inferior beings who need a lot of help."
To prepare him for his Christmas among the icebergs and Emperor Penguins, the British Antarctic Survey invited "Max" and his agent, Judy Arnold, to its headquarters for a day's briefing.

They were shown slides of life at Rothera, a small, noisy settlement where colleagues live cheek by jowl for months on end. One geophysicist at the base is an accomplished musician and is bringing her cello this year.

The composer's inspiration is more likely to come from his trips away from the base. He, Arnold, and two younger assistants will either fly to a satellite base in the middle of nowhere or trek by ski and make camp where they choose, just like the old Polar explorers.
Max smiled bravely as Rothera station commander Paul Rose warned them about seasickness on the four-day trip from the Falkland Islands and the dangers of crevasses.

Soon after arrival, new recruits spend a night out to ensure they have the skills to camp safely on their own. A slide showed a man in full snow gear grappling with the metal tubes and canvas of a pyramid tent.
"Does everyone have to put up their own tent?" 62-year-old Arnold asked nervously.
The next slide showed living conditions inside the tent. Very cramped and messy seemed to sum it up. Arnold looked even more unsure about the whole adventure.
"It'll be the most uncomfortable night in your life but also the most luxurious," Rose says. "The most important thing is to get on with your tent partner."
He suggests the two would like to visit Fossil Bluff, "a petrol station in the middle of nowhere".
"It sleeps four and there's a wonderful feel to it. It's the real Antarctic," Rose enthuses as a slide shows a small hut surrounded by snow, imposing cliffs and more snow.
RAISING ANTARCTIC AWARENESS

The symphony, Maxwell Davies' eighth, was the brainchild of the Survey which wanted to raise awareness of the continent in the arts world and mark the 50th anniversary of the film "Scott of the Antarctic".
Vaughan Williams' symphony was based on his score for the film which portrayed the doomed British expedition to the South Pole in 1912.
The survey approached London's Philarmonia Orchestra. It suggested Maxwell Davies who, coincidentally, had attended the premiere of the Vaughan Williams symphony as a schoolboy.

The sequel will have its world premiere in 2001, conducted by the composer. The length of the commission has taken the pressure off a man renowned for his output -- he has published more than 200 works -- and "Max" is entering the project with an open mind.

"I've thought about it but not got very far. I will let the experience slowly sink in," he said. "I won't have much difficulty avoiding ready-made images as the methods of generating musical material there will determine radically different ways of thinking.
"It's become ever clearer it won't be the kind of explorer/lonely/romantic music you hear in Vaughan Williams' symphony.

"There has been a shift of attitude since Vaughan Williams' time when there was a feeling of heroism about going there, people felt up against the forces of nature. My visit has nothing to do with imperialism."
At home in Hoy, Maxwell Davies has no mains water and feeds his fire with peat and driftwood. Daily supplies have to be carried on his back uphill. Neighbours are few and far between.
His isolation, and the magnificent scenery that stretches away from his house, means his music has been strongly influenced by the natural world.

"There will be various kinds of life I have not encountered before and I think I am going to enjoy that enormously. But it will take time to understand how I will use things I experience in the symphony," he said.
What the piece will contain is an expression of Maxwell Davies' concern about the most southerly continent.
"Antarctica is not permanent any more. Some of it is breaking up, it is changing very fast and the effect could be quite enormous on all of us.

"One feels guilty about going at all as one is polluting, contributing to ozone layer depletion, mucking up the ecology of the place. These new awarenesses have got to come through -- but how to do it, I don't know yet."
